summary_paragraph: A 54-year-old woman with a complex history of Crohn’s disease, short bowel syndrome, and multiple prior surgeries was readmitted for worsening abdominal pain, bilious vomiting, and inability to pass gas, consistent with a partial bowel obstruction on a background of chronic inflammation. She required NG tube decompression, which was frequently dislodged, necessitating repeated replacements. IV hydromorphone was used for pain control, with a gradual transition to oral medications by discharge. A central line was placed for access but was later replaced due to suspected line-related fevers. Hypokalemia, initially resistant to repletion, resolved with reduced NG output. She slowly advanced to a soft diet, began passing gas and having bowel movements, and her anxiety was managed with diazepam taper and restart of citalopram. She was discharged home on oral antibiotics, pain medications, and anxiolytics with close outpatient follow-up.
